query: For initially solid iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles examined across the premelting and melting regime, limited understanding of their thermal response constrains interpretation of application limits and high-temperature synthesis, where cooling must consolidate the solid solution. Prior studies of Ag, Au, Al, and Pd nanoparticles established that nanoscale phase-transition behavior can differ markedly among particle systems, but findings from single-metal particles do not resolve the response of chemically complex nanoparticles. Work on bimetallic particles further demonstrated that chemical complexity can produce varied configurations, while research on high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles remains sparse and has not established the governing physics for this composition. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its premelting and melting behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline particle, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, prior findings that support it, and an observation that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Local compositional inhomogeneities in Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles create microregions with distinct melting points, causing partial melting onset below the bulk melting temperature and driving a two-stage transition where these lower-melting zones liquefy first, subsequently coalescing into a fully molten state.
generation.material_initial_state: As-synthesized, nominally single-phase Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles with sub-10-nm sizes and minor compositional fluctuations.
generation.intervention: In situ heating from ambient to above the bulk melting temperature, combined with deliberate variations in composition (e.g., partial substitution of one element).
generation.conditions: A range of heating rates (slow ~1 K/s vs. rapid >104 K/s) is applied during in situ high-resolution TEM and synchrotron XRD measurements, tracking early premelting and the complete phase transition.
generation.structural_mediator: Spatially varying chemistry and bonding (local compositional inhomogeneity) within each nanoparticle.
generation.mechanism: These local chemical variations create zones with lower energetic barriers to melting, promoting early nucleation of liquid within regions of favored composition. As temperature rises further, the molten regions expand and coalesce, completing the transition to a uniform liquid phase.
generation.predicted_outcome: In Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles, localized liquid pockets will appear at lower temperatures relative to simpler reference particles, and their growth will correlate with the most compositionally disparate domains. In more uniform or single-element nanoparticles, partial melting will be significantly delayed and less extensive.
generation.baseline: Single-metal or basic bimetallic nanoparticles of similar size, which undergo melting near their standard bulk melting points and display less pronounced premelting phenomena.
generation.boundary: For significantly altered compositions (e.g., near-binary or far from ideal high-entropy ratios), or for larger particles with reduced surface-driven inhomogeneities, early localized melting may be negligible or absent.
generation.uncertainty: Potentially incomplete knowledge of the nanoscale distribution of elements and the influence of synthesis history on the observed melting profiles.

falsification_experiment.design: Compare Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles to single-metal or binary nanoparticles of the same size. Conduct in situ heating with high-resolution TEM and XRD, mapping chemical composition (EDS/EELS) to identify the onset of liquid phase formation in local regions versus the overall mass.
measurements: Dynamic evolution of diffraction peaks indicating partial vs. complete melting
Elemental distributions during heating by real-time EDS/EELS in TEM
Temperature-dependent DSC curves to compare onset and progression of melting
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If partial melting in the high-entropy nanoparticles does not correlate with local compositional inhomogeneity, or if their melting profile is identical to simpler references without early localized melting pockets, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This simple model of particle formation demonstrates that adding more elements innately promotes a more random nanoparticle, regardless of element interactions. Naturally, this model offers an idealized perspective and does not reflect all experimental details. In reality, there will be distinct mixing enthalpies between the elements. This will introduce a preference for certain structures which is opposed by the limited mobility of atoms. This explains how a rather mixed particle is obtained in the synthesis for a five-element mixture, which is restricted in the binary case, but also sees signs of local segregation in the NMF analysis. The model relates well to the single-source precursor synthesis, where a solid precursor is reduced at moderate temperatures, hence limiting the free mobility. Extending this approach to other syntheses with similar solid, mixed precursors can thus provide a viable way to design new low-temperature approaches for small high entropy alloy nanoparticles. It can further be argued that starting with a high number of different elements favors the exploration of high-entropy material spaces. AbstractThe single-step incorporation of multiple immiscible elements into colloidal high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles has manifold technological potential, but it continues to be a challenge for state-of-the-art synthesis methods. Hence, the development of a synthesis approach by which the chemical composition and phase of colloidal HEA nanoparticles can be controlled could lead to a new pool of nanoalloys with unparalleled functionalities. Herein, this study reports the single-step synthesis of colloidal CoCrFeMnNi HEA nanoparticles with targeted equimolar stoichiometry and diameters less than 5 nm by liquid-phase, ultrashort-pulsed laser ablation of the consolidated and heat-treated micropowders of the five constituent metals. Further, the scalability of the process with an unprecedented productivity of 3 grams of colloidal HEA nanoparticles per hour is demonstrated. Electrochemical analysis reveals a unique redox behavior of the particles' surfaces in an alkaline environment and a potential for future application as a heterogeneous catalyst for the oxygen evolution reaction. chosen.why: This approach most directly tests the governing physical mechanisms of premelting and melting for multicomponent nanoparticles by combining real-time atomic-scale observation with a computational model. It targets the previously unexplained behavior and clarifies how chemical complexity shapes phase transformations, fulfilling the specific question of identifying a single mechanistic hypothesis for the observed premelting and melting response in Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
